Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define the core components of leadership and leadership development.
Assess the state of leadership in orthopaedic surgery.
Identify leadership development strategies in modern health care and orthopaedic surgery,
from the classroom to the operating room and, eventually, to the boardroom.
Background
Leadership often refers to the act of managing or overseeing via official title or rank.
In practical application, leadership is required at all levels and consists not only of leading
down (as traditionally viewed, to subordinates) but also of leading across (leading
peers/colleagues) and up (managing superiors within an organization).


Background
For orthopaedic surgeons, leadership encompasses formal/official titles in an
organization (ie, service chief, residency director, chairperson) but also unofficial actions
in daily context (leading the surgical team or ambulatory care team). Leadership skills, in
combination with emotional intelligence capabilities, often are more directly responsible
for career success than traditional metrics of intelligence.1,2 Despite the importance of
leadership in career success, this topic is largely ignored in traditional medical education,
including medical school and postgraduate training. Therefore, many physicians have
difficulty developing critical leadership skills, which impedes their career development
and ability to affect the organization.3,4
In addition, as healthcare organizations continue to expand in scale and complexity,
leadership skills will become more critical for orthopaedic surgeons to master to be
successful in the practice and healthcare system.5 Although leadership can be learned
on the job, common principles can be learned and must be appreciated.
Understanding Leadership
Many different frameworks for modern leadership thinking
Leadership is the accomplishment of a goal through the direction of human assistants6
Positive or negative styles of leadership

Understanding Leadership
One challenge in teaching leadership is that it is an inexact science, dependent on
underlying personality traits and characteristics; however, leadership truly is an
evolutionary process because these skills can be taught and iterated upon throughout
the course of an orthopaedic surgeon’s career. All orthopaedic surgeons gained
admission into medical school with a baseline level of leadership, whether through
academic pursuits, athletic teams, or community/volunteer endeavors. In addition, their
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Leadership Development
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
2/12

progression through residency stages inherently incorporates increasing levels of
leadership because junior residents guide and oversee medical students, senior
residents guide junior residents, and faculty/attendings oversee all trainees on the team.
However, progression through these stages in training typically is assured without any
formal leadership training or skills assessment. Therefore, orthopaedic trainees do not
benefit from understanding what it takes to be a proficient leader compared with an
ineffective or negative leader.
Many frameworks for leadership have been established. One popular framework is that
described by John C. Maxwell, which consists of the Five Levels of Leadership.7 Level 1,
the most baseline and primary level, consists of leadership through official position.
Leaders in this level exert influence through the sheer nature of their appointed
position, and followers act strictly because of this appointment. This is the lowest level of
leadership because it requires only an appointment to exert influence as a leader. Level
2 leaders exert influence through permission. Followers of this type of leader act
because the leader has developed interpersonal relationships with the team. These
relationships lead to mutual trust, which in turn lead to action with common goals. Level
3 leaders lead through production. These leaders not only motivate subordinates to act
but also produce results with respect to productivity. In addition to following these
leaders because of interpersonal relationships and trust, subordinates act because of
the leader’s track record of results. Level 4 leaders exert influence through people
development and growth of other leaders within the organization. These leaders amplify
their effect by helping create leaders who can, in turn, produce results and achievement.
Finally, Level 5 leaders represent the pinnacle of leadership. These leaders achieve
maximum productivity and efficiency via lifelong investment in people development.
Level 5 leaders are at the top of their organizations and industries based on a track
record of developing Level 4 leaders. Although physicians can achieve this level of
leadership, level 5 leaders are rare in organizations or industries.
Leadership involves motivating others to act with common goals for the team or
organization. This motivation may be negative or positive.8 In his perspective on
leadership, Dr. Stu Weinstein describes examples of these traits. Negative traits consist
of leadership through intimidation or claims of being all-knowing. Dr. Weinstein further
characterizes good leaders as good listeners who “listen 80% of the time and speak no
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
3/12

more than 20% of the time.” Therefore, positive leadership traits consist of staying
principled and focused on the greater good of the organization rather than the self and
being inclusive.
Current State of Leadership Within Orthopaedic Surgery
As clinicians progress through the leadership ranks, more time is spent in managerial activities
with consequent declines in clinical activities.4,9
Twelve factors confer success for academic medicine leaders:2
Leadership congruency, leadership skills, emotional intelligence, communication skills,
development of a departmental vision, a strong executive leadership team, professional
development, renewable resources, business acumen, personnel management, change
management, and defining success
Leadership development is further complicated by the complex and evolving medicolegal
landscape and the prevalence of defensive medicine practices.9
Leaders also must be conscientious of sex and racial/ethnicity gaps prevalent in US
orthopaedics.

Current State of Leadership Within Orthopaedic Surgery
In most orthopaedic settings, the pinnacle of leadership is represented by department
chairs or group directors. As many as 50% (and in many cases more) of these leaders’
workweek is devoted to nonclinical tasks. These tasks include faculty/group
management, goal setting, strategic vision, operational oversight, mentorship, and many
other tasks. In large groups and healthcare systems, a leader’s efficacy largely depends
on his or her ability to break down bureaucratic barriers and red tape to affect change
and growth in the orthopaedic group or department. In addition, these leaders must
determine how to encourage innovation and risk-taking in a traditionally risk-averse
environment.10
Academic medical systems pose unique challenges for leaders. In private practice (and
even employed models), an increasing emphasis is on the bottom line. This equates to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Leadership Development
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
4/12

compensation models centered on productivity. In academic settings, the leader must
balance clinical productivity as well as academic productivity, department service, and
hospital/healthcare system service. The leader also must determine how to fairly
distribute resources (eg, midlevel providers) in such systems, which do not rely on
individual practitioner collection systems.
To gain credibility, surgeons face dual measures of success. In addition to demonstrating
sound leadership traits, surgeons must first demonstrate clinical proficiency in the
clinical setting and in the operating room. Such proficiency makes it easier for a
surgeon’s peers to follow.11 Surgeon leaders also must stay active in clinical activities
because this continued presence will keep them abreast of day-to-day challenges faced
by the staff and faculty. Naturally, surgeon leaders must exemplify standards of ethics
and cultural sensitivity.
Many leaders are born from disadvantageous circumstances, such as times of
administrative turmoil or poor financial or clinical performance in a given department or
group. Leaders can emerge from these situations if they help the group or organization
right the ship.12 These leaders tend to be creative and produce results that improve the
underlying situation. This behavior is in contrast to the status quo of criticizing the
current situation and being mired in inactivity.
Orthopaedic leaders also must contend with the lack of diversity in sex and
race/ethnicity present in orthopaedics. One method to address this issue involves
recruiting female and minority applicants for orthopaedic residency programs.13 Such
recruitment is contingent on a culture of inclusivity that may be lacking in groups that
are unidimensional in race and sex. Leaders can help actively promote inclusive cultures
through promotion of educational programs, targeted mentorship, and other such
efforts directed to the group or department.
Effective orthopaedic leadership also can help the organization improve quality.14
Leaders must identify quality and safety as key initiatives for the group and organization
and further establish clear goals and expectations. Leaders also should promote
initiatives around quality that are aligned with these goals. This includes creating a
culture of quality improvement, promotion of quality programs, and partnership with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Leadership Development
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
5/12

the hospital for major initiatives (ie, clinical pathways and multidisciplinary clinics for
joint replacement patients). Successful quality and safety goal-setting (and achievement)
will help the group or department more effectively transition to value-based care
initiatives, such as bundled payment programs and national ranking metrics.
Developing Leadership Skills
Residents face particular challenges in developing leadership skills because they typically have
not been exposed to formal training in this discipline.
Various informal and formal avenues exist by which residents can pursue leadership training.
To be an effective leader, orthopaedic surgeons must make a concerted and persistent effort
to develop leadership skills. This should be an active rather than a passive pursuit.

Developing Leadership Skills
In the business world, managers have many opportunities for leadership development.
This begins with undergraduate and graduate (eg, business school) curricula, which
often include leadership coursework. After employment, numerous formal development
programs are available to provide managers with leadership experience pertinent to
their industry and organization. Contrast this with the experience of an orthopaedic
surgeon, whose undergraduate curriculum consists of premedical coursework focused
on math and science. Typical medical school curricula ignore leadership and
management training, and no training opportunities exist during residency and
fellowship. This deficit in training is exacerbated by the current promotion system in
virtually all residency programs (promotion upon the passing of a year as rather than
being contingent on the demonstration of clinical and leadership skills) and the common
misconception that leadership is inherent or naturally evolves with time and experience.
To develop into great leaders, orthopaedic residents must understand that leadership
training is active and purposeful. In addition, timeless core competencies must be
appreciated, as identified by Clohisy et al during the 2017 American Orthopaedic
Association Critical Issues symposium. These core competencies include integrity,
credibility, effective listening, having a vision of your destination, fairness, humility, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Leadership Development
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
6/12

caring.15 Each of these competencies should be cultivated and developed throughout all
stages of training and are not limited to any particular setting. Several informal and
formal opportunities may help residents succeed in their leadership development.
Informal Avenues for Leadership Development
Mentorship

Mentorship
Mentorship is a common mode of education for orthopaedic residents, especially with
regard to clinical development. Residents should seek out mentors who are recognized
and effective surgeon leaders. The mentorship should consist of regular meetings in
which the trainee can learn the soft and hard skills required to be a successful leader.
For the relationship to be most effective, the mentee should prepare questions for the
mentor to advise upon, and the mentee should be prepared to engage in self-education
as needed. Mentorship may be a valuable resource for underrepresented groups in
orthopaedics, such as female and/or minority surgeons.16 (Video 1)

as a mentor and a mentee. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy

Self-education

Self-education
Numerous resources are available (eg, traditional, electronic, audiobooks) on leadership
development. They routinely are referenced by the business community, and many offer
real-world, practical advice on leadership development. Examples of popular texts are
Extreme Ownership and The Dichotomy of Leadership (Willink), Leaders Eat Last and Find
Your Why (Sinek), books by John C. Maxwell, books about great leaders in history (eg,
Doris Kearns Goodwin’s profiles of presidents Theodore Roosevelt, Franklin Delano
Roosevelt, and Abraham Lincoln), and many others. Aspiring leaders also may wish to
review books that focus on business management/team dynamics or on human nature
and effective communication.
Formal Avenues for Leadership Development
Graduate Education

Graduate Education
A common method for leadership development is through additional graduate
coursework.17 This may consist of a formal second degree (eg, Master of Business
Administration) or individual coursework focused on leadership development for
managers. Some orthopaedic training programs may be supportive of residents stepping
away for 1 or 2 years to pursue a formal degree. These programs also are available to
orthopaedic providers after residency, with many offering weekend-only coursework or
virtual education. One advantage of pursuing a second degree, such as a Master of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:32 PM
AAOS | Leadership Development
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6000015
8/12

Business Administration, is that it signals to the healthcare (and professional) community
that the orthopaedic professional has formally undertaken (and gained competency in)
business administration and leadership coursework.
Organizational Training Programs

Organizational Training Programs
Many organizations, especially large, multidisciplinary healthcare systems, offer
leadership development programs for employed physicians. These may be available to
residents but typically are available only to staff physicians. Such programs may be
invaluable not only in teaching leadership skills but also in connecting surgeons to
organizational leaders they otherwise would not interact with. These connections may
be useful for future initiatives that rely on administrative support.
Society and Subspecialty Leadership Programs

Society and Subspecialty Leadership Programs
Residents should be aware of initiatives from the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons or subspecialty organizations that foster leadership development or leadership
positions. Such opportunities provide residents and surgeons with opportunities to gain
real-world leadership skills even at an early stage in their career.
